Panel 6 is a clean, squared-off half-page: hard gutters return, the layout itself signalling the return of rational daylight. The shift from bleeding, warped panels to rigid geometry should be viscerally felt.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE HORIZONTAL PANEL — fever-dream. Victor and Elizabeth in a moonlit Genevese street rendered in loose, dissolving ink washes. Elizabeth faces us, luminous and full of life, her hair loose, her expression radiant. Victor's arms are wrapped around her from behind, his face pressed toward hers in a first kiss — but his eyes are open and terrified, as if already sensing what is coming. The background architecture — arched doorways, cobblestones — warps subtly at the edges, stones stretching like taffy. Colour palette: silver-white and deep indigo, with one sickly warm candle-gold at the vanishing point. Crosshatched shadows bloom outward from Elizabeth's feet like ink dropped in water. Expressionist distortion: the street bends slightly upward at the horizon as if the world itself is queasy.
panels.narration: I thought I saw Elizabeth — alive, radiant — walking toward me through the streets of Ingolstadt.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM CLOSE-UP — the transformation. Same embrace, but now Elizabeth's face has begun to shift. Her cheek against Victor's is pallid, grey-tinged. Her lips — parted as if to speak — are livid, blue-white, the lips of a corpse. Her eyes have gone glassy, the irises clouding. And beneath her, glimpsed as if through a dissolving veil, is his mother's death-mask: the same face, older, cold, the stillness of the grave wearing Elizabeth's features like a costume. Victor's expression: pure, silent horror — mouth open, no scream yet, the body understanding before the mind. Use dense crosshatching on the transitional face to evoke the texture of old anatomical engravings — a clinical precision made monstrous. The panel border itself fractures at the lower right corner.
panels.narration: Her lips — the first kiss — livid. Cold as the grave. And beneath her face... my mother's.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT CLOSE-UP — Victor's eyes snapping open. Extreme close: just his eyes, the bridge of his nose, and the top of his sweat-drenched brow filling the panel. His eyes are blown wide, pupils dilated to black discs, the whites showing all around — a man wrenched from nightmare into waking terror. Sweat beads on his skin, rendered with fine stippling. The iris catches the trembling flame of an unseen candle — a single warm point of gold in an otherwise cold, blue-black composition. The panel is deliberately cramped, the face pressing against all four borders — claustrophobic, suffocating. This is the hinge between dream and waking.

NEAR FULL-PAGE VERTICAL — the Creature in the doorframe. Pull back to a low-angle shot from Victor's prostrate perspective on the bed, looking up and toward the door. The Creature fills the doorframe entirely — eight feet of assembled flesh, his silhouette eating the doorway, blotting out what little moonlight bled through the corridor beyond. One vast hand is outstretched toward Victor, palm up, as if in entreaty — or threat, the gesture is deliberately ambiguous. His face is illuminated from below by the guttering candle Victor holds up: the watery yellow eyes catch the light and glint, the straight black lips are stretched back in that terrible, unreadable grin. The crosshatching on the Creature's form is dense and directional — lines radiating from his silhouette as if he absorbs rather than reflects light. Victor's arm (holding the candle) enters the frame at the lower corner, trembling. Around the Creature's feet: deep shadow, pure black ink, pooling like water.
dialogue: Victor (small, breathless): "...his eyes fixed on me. His jaws opened — "
panels.narration: He had followed me. Of course he had.

panels.visual_direction: NARROW HORIZONTAL STRIP — Victor in flight. A long, low panel: Victor seen from behind and above, sprinting down the dark staircase of his lodgings, a pale figure in a nightshirt, the candle extinguished, one hand trailing the banister. The staircase is rendered in steep, Caligari-esque diagonal — the steps almost vertical with perspective, the walls leaning inward as if the building itself is closing around him. Motion lines blur his lower legs. The shadows behind him are enormous and absolute, the Creature implied rather than shown — just a vast darkness at the top of the stair. The sole light source: a pale grey square of pre-dawn sky glimpsed at the bottom of the stairwell, impossibly far away.
panels.narration: I ran. I did not stop until the street received me.

panels.visual_direction: CLEAN HALF-PAGE — morning. Hard cut. The panel border is sharp and perfectly squared — a deliberate visual reset. Warm morning light floods a doorstep: honey-gold and amber replace all the cold indigo and sickly green of the preceding panels. Henry Clerval stands in the open doorway, travel-dusty, bags at his feet, hat in hand — his face open, smiling, entirely alive. He looks directly at Victor (and us) with an expression of uncomplicated delight and mild concern. Victor is just visible at the panel's left edge, his back to us, his posture that of a man who has been standing in the cold for hours — but his head is turning toward Clerval, the first turn toward warmth. The background is an Ingolstadt street in early morning light: ordinary, detailed, real. No distortion. The world has snapped back into place.
dialogue: Clerval: "Victor! My dear friend — at last. You look as though you haven't slept in a week."
Victor (barely audible): "Henry... you came."
panels.narration: And just like that — as if morning itself had sent him — Henry Clerval arrived. And the night, for a moment, was over.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page 1: three stacked panels of diminishing width — a wide establishing shot, a narrow horizontal grief close-up, and a slim landscape strip of the storm-wracked road. Page 2: opens with a full-page SPLASH (Panel 4) — the lightning-revealed Creature on the crags with Victor a tiny stricken figure below — then two tight panels beneath or on a facing page: Panel 5 a close-up on Victor's face, Panel 6 pure darkness with fading thunder text. The splash must dominate. Heavy Doré-style crosshatching throughout; watercolor bleeds in blue-black and sickly yellow only where lightning or lantern light touches skin.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE ESTABLISHING SHOT. The gates of Geneva at night, seen from outside the city walls. Lantern light bleeds through iron bars onto wet cobblestones. Victor Frankenstein stands before the gates — tall, lean, coat travel-worn — his back to us, shoulders bowed under invisible weight. Beyond the gates, the silhouette of a city that does not yet know its grief. Above, the sky is bruised purple-black, the first veins of lightning forking over the distant Jura peaks. The composition frames Victor as miniature against massive stone and sky — a man arriving too late, already dwarfed by what awaits him. Crosshatched stonework; the lantern a smear of jaundiced yellow in the dark.
panels.narration: I had been five years absent. I returned to Geneva a different man — or perhaps, at last, the man I had always been making.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT CLOSE-UP. Victor's face in three-quarter profile, lit from below by a held lantern — the worst light for a face, making hollows of his cheeks and sockets of his eyes. He is beautiful still, but the beauty is cracking: grief has arrived before understanding. His jaw is set. His eyes are wet and fixed on something off-panel — something he cannot yet look away from. A single tear track catches the lantern gold. The background dissolves into Mignola-style ink void — only the face, the light, the grief. No dialogue. The panel border is thin and slightly uneven, as if drawn by a shaking hand.
panels.narration: William. My little William. Strangled. The marks of fingers on his throat.

panels.visual_direction: SLIM HORIZONTAL LANDSCAPE STRIP — almost a letterbox. Victor walks the mountain road outside the city, heading toward Plainpalais. The path cuts diagonally from lower-left to upper-right, drawing the eye upward into the storm. The Jura mountains loom on the right, barely distinguishable from the sky — both are the same churning black-grey. Lightning illuminates the scene in partial white: we see the road, the rocks, the lone figure moving. The strip format makes the world feel compressed, the sky oppressive, the path endless. Wind-bent pines lean inward over Victor like accusatory witnesses.
panels.narration: The storm descended as I neared the scene of the murder. As though the sky itself had been waiting for me.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-PAGE SPLASH. This is the image the entire scene has been building toward. COMPOSITION: Victor occupies the bottom fifth of the page — a small, dark figure on the mountain path, face tilted upward, coat blown horizontal by the gale, lantern extinguished. He is rendered in fine crosshatch detail but dwarfed. Above him, filling the remaining four-fifths of the page: the Creature. A lightning bolt — white, jagged, occupying the upper-right diagonal — throws everything into stark chiaroscuro. The Creature clings to the near-vertical rockface with one enormous hand, body angled outward as if defying gravity. He is MONSTROUS in scale: eight feet of assembled humanity, yellow-skinned, the proportions slightly wrong in the way that only becomes apparent when compared to the tiny Victor below. His face is turned downward — not toward Victor, but toward the valley, toward the city — and wears an expression of terrible, unreadable blankness. The lightning makes his pale eyes incandescent. Watercolor washes: electric blue-white for the lightning field, dead yellow-ochre bleeding across the Creature's skin, absolute ink-black for the crags and sky. Victor's upturned face is a pale oval of pure horror. No speech bubbles break this panel. The sound effects are part of the art.
panels.narration: One flash. One terrible, sufficient flash.

panels.visual_direction: CLOSE-UP on Victor's face — now facing us directly, lantern dropped and forgotten, both hands raised slightly as if to ward off the vision. His expression is not simple terror: it is the specific horror of confirmation, of a fear so long suppressed that its arrival feels like recognition. Eyes wide, pupils contracted to pinpoints by the lightning. Mouth slightly open — not a scream, a breath caught and not released. The crosshatching deepens around his eyes and jaw, expressionist shadows carving his face into something almost skeletal. Behind him, already, the darkness is returning — the lightning afterimage fading from the sky, leaving only the deep bruised purple of the storm. He is alone again. He knows.
dialogue: He is the murderer. There can be no doubt.

panels.visual_direction: NEAR-BLACK PANEL. Almost the full panel is ink — a void of Mignola blackness. At the very bottom, a thin sliver of grey suggests the mountain road. In the upper half, only the faintest ghost-suggestion of the rockface remains, the Creature's shape already dissolved back into the dark — visible only as a slightly different texture in the black, a presence that might be imagined. The lightning is gone. This panel should feel like the moment after a candle is snuffed: the image burned onto the retina, fading. Thunder rolls its final note. The word WILLIAM appears in a small narration box — just the name, nothing else — set in italic, lower-left, as if whispered into the dark.
panels.narration: William.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page 1: Three panels — a wide establishing shot spanning the full width at top, then two equal panels below. Page 2: Three panels — two equal panels on top, then a single wide cinematic panel anchoring the bottom, bleeding to the page edges. Heavy black gutters throughout to enforce the sense of enclosure and dread. The final panel should feel airless and vast simultaneously — a grey void with a single small figure.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE ESTABLISHING SHOT — full-width panel. Interior of an 18th-century Genevan courtroom, rendered in dense crosshatched ink with Doré-like architectural detail. Vaulted stone arches press down from above, exaggerating the ceiling's weight. The public gallery is a sea of dark, hostile faces — mouths tight, eyes hard — rendered in loose expressionist strokes so they blur into a single organism of accusation. Centre frame: Justine Moritz stands in the wooden dock, small but utterly still. She is lit by a single shaft of cold light falling from a high window — the only true light source in the panel. Her posture is dignified, hands folded, chin level. She does not flinch. Victor sits in the upper gallery to the far left, already turning his face away, a hunched shadow half-hidden behind a stone pillar. Alphonse sits rigidly beside him, grey-faced with grief. The composition draws the eye along a strong diagonal from the hostile crowd down to Justine's isolated, luminous figure.
panels.narration: Geneva. The Hall of Justice. They had already decided.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT — Elizabeth rises to speak, viewed from slightly below, so she seems to stand against the dark vault of the ceiling. Her golden hair catches the courtroom's weak light like a struck match. Her white dress is radiant and wrong — a figure of warmth in a room built from stone and condemnation. Her expression is fierce with love, eyes bright with unshed tears, one hand pressed to her chest and the other outstretched toward the judges — unseen, off-panel. Around her the gallery faces turn to stare, cold and unmoved. Expressionist watercolour wash: a faint aureole of amber behind Elizabeth that bleeds into grey at the edges — warmth already failing.
dialogue: She is innocent. I have known her since childhood. She is incapable of this.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT CLOSE-UP — Victor's hands. He has buried his face in them. His fingers press into his brow so hard the knuckles whiten. The hands are detailed with almost anatomical precision — tendons raised, nails bitten. Between his fingers we glimpse only a sliver of his face: one eye, open, staring at nothing. The eye is dry. The horror is too deep for tears. Heavy Mignola-style shadow engulfs the upper half of the frame; the hands emerge from darkness into a sickly pale half-light. No background — just a void of black ink pressing in.
panels.narration: I knew. I knew, and I said nothing. The words were in my throat and I swallowed them like poison.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM CLOSE-UP — Justine in the dock, now addressing the court directly. She looks out with an expression of absolute composure — not cold, but resolved, the face of someone who has made peace with an outcome she cannot change. There is immense sorrow in her eyes but no self-pity. Behind her, the hostile faces of the crowd are rendered as smeared, almost featureless shapes — ink blooms — as if seen through water or the distortion of a grief-stricken mind. She is the only figure in sharp focus in the entire panel.
dialogue: God knows how entirely I am innocent. I do not ask you to believe me. I ask only that He remembers it.

panels.visual_direction: VERTICAL PANEL — tall and narrow, like a coffin stood upright. Grey pre-dawn exterior. The scaffold stands against a milk-white sky, crosshatched in fine lines that make the sky itself feel like a steel engraving — cold, unyielding, without mercy. Justine stands at the top of the scaffold steps, her back to us. She is small. The architecture of death dwarfs her. A priest stands nearby, head bowed. The crowd below is a dark mass, featureless. Justine's head is slightly raised — she is looking at the sky, not the crowd. Expressionist watercolour: the white sky bleeds to a faint, bruised yellow at the horizon — the colour of a dying candle.
panels.narration: Dawn. The colour of nothing.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH CINEMATIC PANEL — bleeds to page edges. Split composition: LEFT HALF — outside the city walls, Victor stands alone on a dirt path. He faces away from Geneva, away from us. His coat is pulled tight. He is very still. His silhouette is hunched, slightly bent, as though something heavy has been laid across his shoulders. The city walls rise behind him, massive and dark. RIGHT HALF — the same grey sky continues unbroken across the panel divide, vast and indifferent. From somewhere beyond the walls, barely suggested, rises a distant sound — rendered as a typographic SOUND EFFECT in faint, crumbling letterforms, as if the word itself is disintegrating. The two halves of the panel are separated not by a gutter but by the unbroken sky — Victor and the act are in the same world, the same moment, with no boundary between his silence and its consequence.
panels.narration: I, the true murderer — felt the never-dying worm alive in my bosom. There was no consolation. There could be none.

panel_scripts.scene_title: Confrontation on the Glacier — The Creature Speaks
panel_scripts.layout_notes: This scene should feel like a descent from the vast to the intimate — open with a breathtaking full-width establishing shot, then compress the panels as the emotional weight closes in. Panels 1 and 2 should span the full page width to establish the sublime scale. Panels 3–5 are tighter, stacked or split vertically, driving the reader into the faces of both figures. Panel 6 returns to a wide shot but inverted in tone — no longer awe-inspiring, now isolating and sorrowful. Use heavy crosshatch inking for the glacier's jagged seracs; let ink bleed into loose grey-blue watercolor washes for sky and shadow. Figures should be rendered with precise anatomical weight against semi-abstracted backgrounds. The Creature must never read as a monster in close-up — his face must carry grief, not malice.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH PANORAMIC ESTABLISHING SHOT. The Mer de Glace glacier stretches across the entire panel — a frozen ocean of shattered seracs, deep blue-black crevasses, and churning ice formations beneath a vast, oppressive grey sky. Mont Blanc looms in the far distance, half-swallowed by cloud. In the dead centre of this inhuman landscape, almost lost in the immensity, two tiny figures face each other: Victor Frankenstein — slight, dark-coated, braced against the wind — and the Creature, towering nearly a foot taller, his ragged silhouette unmistakable. The scale must be crushing. These are insects before eternity. Doré-style engraving detail on the ice formations; the sky bleeds into expressionist watercolor — churning greys and cold whites.
panels.narration: Below Mont Blanc, on the frozen sea they call the Mer de Glace — the world offers no witness. Only ice. Only sky. Only the two of us.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE SHOT, ground level, dramatic diagonal composition. The Creature advances across the ice toward Victor — his movement is swift and purposeful, not shambling. His massive frame is dressed in layers of torn, filthy fabric, his long black hair whipping in the alpine wind. His proportions are subtly wrong — eight feet of assembled flesh, limbs too long, gait too fluid for something so vast. Victor stands his ground at the right edge of the panel, small but rigid with fury and horror, one hand raised as if to halt the approach. The glacier's jagged seracs frame both figures like the teeth of a trap closing. Low camera angle makes the Creature loom against the sky. Ink is heavy and dark; the Creature's silhouette bleeds into shadow.
dialogue: Victor (shouted into the wind): Devil! Do you dare approach me? Begone — or let us settle this in combat!
sound_effects: CRUNCH CRUNCH — heavy footfalls on packed ice

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT — the Creature stops. He is perhaps ten feet from Victor now, and he does not raise his hands in threat. He raises them in a gesture of awful supplication — palms outward, arms slightly spread, a posture borrowed from religious painting. His face is turned toward Victor fully for the first time. The face must be rendered with unflinching anatomical precision AND with emotional intelligence: the watery yellow eyes are not monstrous here — they are wounded. The dun-white complexion, the straight black lips, the patchwork of his assembled skin — all present, but organised by an expression of anguished restraint. He is holding himself back. He is begging to be heard. Victor in the foreground, right, seen from behind — his coat rigid, his fists clenched. The gap between them is a chasm.
dialogue: The Creature: I expected this. All men hate the wretched — how much more must I be hated, who am miserable beyond all living things.

panels.visual_direction: CLOSE-UP on the Creature's face — the most important panel in the scene. Fill the frame with him. The yellow eyes are direct, unflinching, glistening — not with animal hunger but with intelligence and grief. The black lips are parted mid-speech. Deep crosshatch inking defines the unnatural seams of his skin, the hollow of his cheeks, the terrible beauty of a face that should not exist. But the EXPRESSION overrides the horror: this is the face of someone who has rehearsed this moment a thousand times and is terrified it will go wrong. A thin watercolor wash — cold blue-grey — bleeds around the edges of the panel, framing his face in a halo of desolation. No background. Psychology only.
dialogue: The Creature: Yet you, my creator — you detest and spurn me. Your own creature. Bound to you by ties only death can break.

panels.visual_direction: TWO-SHOT, tight, confrontational. Victor and the Creature face each other in profile — Victor on the left, the Creature on the right, their faces separated by only a few inches of white space on the page. Victor's expression is a war of emotions: revulsion, fury, and — just beginning to surface, cracking through like ice — recognition. He cannot look away. The Creature's gaze is level, steady, the pleading replaced for a moment by something harder: moral authority. The wind catches both their coats. Behind them the glacier continues, indifferent and vast. The panel border should feel compressed, claustrophobic — all that immensity reduced to the distance between two faces.
dialogue: The Creature: Do your duty towards me. And I will do mine towards you — and the rest of mankind.
panels.narration: I had fashioned him capable of reason. I had not considered he would turn it upon me.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE SHOT — pulling back to the panoramic view of Panel 1, but now the two figures have stopped. They are still. The Creature has not attacked. Victor has not fled. They stand on the glacier in the hush after the first words — two solitary, implausible figures in an infinite white void. The sky above presses down. The ice stretches in every direction. There is no warmth here, no comfort, no witness. But the reader understands: something has shifted. The confrontation has become a conversation. The monster is waiting. The creator has no choice but to listen. Ink the foreground ice in sharp, heavy detail; let the background dissolve into pale, exhausted watercolor wash — a world that has run out of colour.
panels.narration: On the glacier, in the silence between us, I felt the full weight of what I had made. And for the first time — I was afraid of something worse than his violence. I was afraid he was right.

panel_scripts.scene_title: The Creature's Education — Watching the De Laceys
panel_scripts.layout_notes: This scene spans a single page of 6 panels. The dominant visual motif is INSIDE vs. OUTSIDE — warm amber tones within the cottage, cold blue-black in the hovel. Panels 1 and 6 are full-width horizontal strips (establishing and closing). Panels 2, 3, and 4 form a tight triptych in the middle tier — narrow vertical panels of equal width, like slits of light through a wall. Panel 5 is a large square, nearly half a page, centered on Safie's arrival. The crack in the hovel wall acts as a recurring visual frame-within-a-frame. Heavy crosshatched ink on the exterior; loose amber watercolor wash floods the interior. The Creature's eye — massive, watery, pale yellow — should appear in at least three panels, always partially obscured, always watching.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH HORIZONTAL ESTABLISHING STRIP. Exterior view, dusk. A low stone hovel, barely visible against a snowline forest rendered in dense Doré-style crosshatching — black spruce, diagonal shadow, oppressive sky. A faint amber glow bleeds from a single crack in the shared wall between the hovel and the adjoining cottage. The cottage windows pulse with warm light; the hovel is a tomb by comparison. The Creature is not yet visible — only his enormous silhouette, hunched and still, pressed against the wall. The scale contrast is immediate: even crouching, he dwarfs the structure. Caption box in upper left, handwritten-style serif font.
panels.narration: For months, I did not exist. I only watched.

panels.visual_direction: NARROW VERTICAL PANEL — left of triptych. Extreme close-up: the Creature's eye fills almost the entire panel, pressed to the crack in the planking. The eye is enormous, pale yellow, with a watery luminescence — anatomically precise, subtly inhuman, deeply sorrowful. The iris catches the amber light from inside. Around the eye: the dark, textured skin — dun-white, crosshatched with fine black lines suggesting the musculature beneath. The crack itself bisects the panel diagonally, a thin blade of warm light cutting across cold shadow. The Creature is invisible except for this one impossible eye. The effect is voyeuristic and tragic simultaneously.
panels.narration: Through that narrow gap — a whole world.

panels.visual_direction: NARROW VERTICAL PANEL — center of triptych. The Creature's POV through the crack: inside the cottage, Felix sits close to a guttering candle, reading aloud from a heavy book, his finger tracing the lines. Agatha leans over her embroidery nearby, face tilted with quiet attention. The blind father, De Lacey, sits in his chair with his guitar across his lap, head slightly raised — listening. The scene is rendered in loose amber watercolor wash over precise ink linework: faces carry real tenderness. The warmth is almost painful. The crack's edges — raw wood, splintered — frame the image like a wound in a wall. Outside the crack: pure black.
dialogue: Felix (reading aloud): '...and so mankind, in all its striving, remains a creature of habit and of hope...'

panels.visual_direction: NARROW VERTICAL PANEL — right of triptych. Interior focus shifts: De Lacey's hands on the guitar strings, rendered with anatomical precision — aged, articulate hands that know by touch what his eyes cannot give him. The music is implied through small radiating curved lines in the Mignola style, suggestive rather than literal. Behind him, just barely visible, the enormous knuckles of the Creature's hand, pressed flat against the outer wall in the darkness. The juxtaposition is the whole of the panel's meaning: the blind man's beautiful, human hands; the monster's vast, hidden ones. Both reaching toward something neither can name.
panels.narration: He could not see me. Of all of them — only he could not see me.

panels.visual_direction: LARGE SQUARE PANEL — nearly half-page. Safie's arrival. Safie stands in the open cottage doorway, snow on her dark hair, a lantern held before her. She is rendered in a sudden explosion of warm colour — crimson shawl, deep amber lantern-light — that floods the panel like a lit match dropped into darkness. Felix has risen from his chair; Agatha has pressed her hands to her mouth in joy. Even old De Lacey has turned his face toward the sound and warmth. In the lower-right foreground — barely a sliver of the panel — the crack in the wall, and behind it, one enormous pale eye, wide and stricken. The Creature watches the scene with an expression caught between wonder and devastation. The watercolor bleeds here should be the richest, warmest in the entire scene: Safie is colour itself entering a grey world.
dialogue: Safie: "I have come so far. I hope — I hope I am not unwelcome."
panels.narration: Colour. I had not known colour could feel like sound.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH HORIZONTAL CLOSING STRIP. Night. The cottage windows now glow with double warmth — Safie's presence felt even from outside. The Creature sits alone in the hovel, back against the cold wall, knees drawn to his chest — a posture simultaneously childlike and grotesque given his enormous frame. In his hands: a single fallen leaf, held with impossible delicacy between fingers the size of sausages. His face is turned slightly upward. The expression is the most important element: not horror, not rage — something raw and ruined, a grief not yet given a name. The ink here returns to dense crosshatching; the watercolor wash is cold blue-grey. The amber light from the cottage falls in one thin stripe across the Creature's face — illuminating his watery eyes. Caption box, lower right.
panels.narration: Books gave me language. Language gave me thought. And thought gave me the one question I could not survive: Was I a monster — or only a man whom no one would allow to be otherwise?

panel_scripts.scene_title: Rejection by the De Laceys — The Creature Turns
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six-panel layout across two pages. Page 1: Panel 1 is a wide horizontal establishing shot spanning the full page width (top tier). Below it, Panels 2 and 3 share equal space in the second tier — Panel 2 slightly larger. Page 2: Panel 4 is a massive, near-full-width panel of violent chaos dominating the top two-thirds. Panel 5 is a narrow vertical strip on the right — the Creature in the doorway. Panel 6 is a wide, mournful horizontal at the bottom — the forest howl. Use heavy ink shadows throughout; the warm amber of the cottage interior should bleed and collapse into cold blue-black as the scene progresses. Panel borders should feel like woodcut frames, slightly rough-edged.

panels.visual_direction: Wide establishing shot of the cottage interior — warm, amber candlelight. Low camera angle looking across the earthen floor. The Creature kneels enormous before the frail, seated blind father, De Lacey — their size contrast is stark and heartbreaking. The Creature's massive, gnarled hands cup the old man's thin ones with extraordinary gentleness. His hideous face — yellow-skinned, black-lipped, pale yellow eyes glistening — is tilted down toward the old man's kind, sightless face in a posture of supplication. Crosshatched ink renders the cottage walls dense with shadow, but a halo of candlelight encircles the two figures like a Renaissance painting — fragile, holy, doomed. The Creature's expression: desperate, aching hope.
dialogue: OLD DE LACEY: "Your voice trembles, friend. Whatever burden you carry — speak it plainly. I have known suffering enough to hear it without flinching."
THE CREATURE: "I have watched over your family these many months. I have loved you — though you do not know it. I have no other friends in all the world."
panels.narration: He had practiced these words ten thousand times in the dark.

panels.visual_direction: Tight two-shot, low angle, intimately close. The Creature's massive, scarred hand — the anatomy exaggerated in the Gothic tradition, knuckles like river stones — rests atop the old man's frail fingers. De Lacey's face in soft half-profile: weathered, gentle, unseeing eyes turned slightly upward. His expression is one of open compassion, no trace of revulsion. The warmth of the scene should feel almost unbearable in its fragility — watercolor amber washes bleeding at the edges into encroaching darkness. This is the closest the Creature will ever come to being seen as a man.
dialogue: OLD DE LACEY: "Then you are not alone. Sit with me."
THE CREATURE: "You cannot see me. If you could—"
OLD DE LACEY: "I have no need of eyes to know a suffering soul."

panels.visual_direction: Exterior — the cottage door from outside, a small panel rendered in cold blues and blacks. Through the frost-edged window, the amber glow of the interior is visible — a small warm rectangle in a vast, dark forest. Felix, Agatha, and Safie approach along the path, figures small against the looming treeline. Felix is slightly ahead; Safie's hand is in Agatha's. Their faces are not yet visible — they are silhouettes of normalcy walking toward something that will unmake them. A German Expressionist diagonal — the cottage roof, the tree line — pulls the eye toward the lit window like a blade.
panels.narration: He did not hear them coming.

panels.visual_direction: Explosive full-width chaos panel — the door has been flung open. Diagonal composition, everything tilted, reality itself lurching. Felix is center-frame, face a mask of screaming, primal horror — mouth wide, veins in his neck, a walking staff raised above his head mid-strike. The Creature recoils from the blow but does NOT raise his hands to defend himself — his arms hang open at his sides, face turned to receive the strike, an expression of shattered disbelief rather than anger. Agatha collapses in the background, Safie has fled through the open door. Old De Lacey has risen from his chair, hands outstretched, calling out — but Felix cannot hear him. Heavy crosshatching fractures the candlelight into jagged shards. The warmth of the interior is visually shattered — ink bleeds black across the amber wash.
dialogue: FELIX: "GET AWAY FROM HIM!"
OLD DE LACEY: "Felix — Felix, stop — he is a friend—"
panels.narration: He could have broken Felix like dry wood. He stood and received the blows instead.

panels.visual_direction: Narrow vertical panel — the Creature stands in the open doorway, silhouetted against the forest dark. He faces outward, back to the viewer, his enormous frame filling the door frame entirely. His arms are raised slightly at his sides — not threatening, not fleeing, simply open. A gesture of surrender. The warm light of the cottage falls across his back, but his shadow stretches forward into the cold dark beyond the threshold. His head is slightly bowed. The cottage interior behind him is empty — De Lacey's overturned chair, the extinguished candle on its side, a thin curl of smoke. Everything is abandonment.
dialogue: THE CREATURE (whispered, no bubble — caption only): "I had good dispositions. Where they ought to have seen a friend — they saw only a monster."
panels.narration: He did not look back.

panels.visual_direction: Final panel — wide, panoramic, merciless. The forest at night rendered in the full Doré tradition: vast, indifferent trees receding into absolute darkness, their bare branches a dense crosshatched canopy blotting out the sky. The Creature stands alone in a small clearing, face tilted upward, mouth open in a silent howl — or perhaps it is not silent, perhaps the sound is too large for speech bubbles, too large for the page. His arms are outstretched to the empty sky. He is tiny against the trees and enormous against everything human. No warmth anywhere in this panel — only blue-black ink washes and the white of his upturned face. In the far background, just barely visible: the dark shape of the cottage, a single extinguished window.
panels.narration: From that moment he declared everlasting war — against the species, and above all, against the one who had made him and sent him forth into this insupportable misery.

panel_scripts.scene_title: The Creature's Demand — Make Me a Companion
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page 1: Panel 1 runs the full page width as a deep horizontal establishing shot (approx. one-third page height). Panels 2 and 3 share the lower two-thirds — Panel 2 a tall vertical occupying two-thirds width left, Panel 3 a tight square inset at right. Page 2: Panel 4 opens as a wide horizontal bleeding to both edges (approx. half page height). Panel 5 sits below-left as a near-square close-up. Panel 6 occupies the bottom-right as a vertical, mirroring Panel 2's shape but inverted in emotional register — where Panel 2 climbs with threat, Panel 6 collapses into surrender. All panels use heavy ink borders that bleed into crosshatched gutter shadows, reinforcing enclosure and inevitability. The gutter space itself should be rendered in deep charcoal wash — no white gutters; the glacier cold must press in from every edge.

panels.visual_direction: Full-width horizontal panel, extreme long shot. The Mer de Glace in failing late-afternoon light — the sky is more void than sky, pressing down in iron-grey and violet. Two tiny figures stand at center frame: the Creature looms nearly a head above Victor, his silhouette massive and ragged against the ice. Between them, only space and the unspeakable scale of the alpine world. Crosshatched ice ridges recede to both edges in Doré-style architectural precision, every ridge-line and crevasse drawn with engraver's exactitude. Wind-driven snow streaks diagonally across the composition from upper-left to lower-right. The two figures are dwarfed, yet every eye gravitates toward them — the only warm, dark shapes in a world of pale indifference. A thin watercolor wash of iron-blue bleeds across the glacier surface, deepening to near-black at the panel's upper corners. No dialogue — only the silence of altitude.
panels.narration: He had followed me to the roof of the world. I had no more excuses left.

panels.visual_direction: Tall vertical panel. Low-angle medium shot looking up at the Creature from Victor's approximate eye-line — making him even more enormous, his proportions subtly distorted in the Expressionist mode. His posture is that of supplication barely held: shoulders forward, massive head inclined, hands open at his sides — not threatening yet, but every line of muscle and tendon in his body suggests how thin the membrane between appeal and fury has grown. His face is rendered with full anatomical horror and terrible humanity simultaneously: watery pale eyes catching the last cold light, straight black lips parted, anguish carved in the deep shadow-channels beneath his cheekbones. The background bleeds to abstracted darkness behind him — only diagonal wind-lines suggest the glacier continues. Ink is heaviest on his silhouette, feathering inward to finer crosshatch on his skin. A Mignola-style bold shadow falls across the lower half of his face, bisecting it between light and dark.
dialogue: THE CREATURE: You must create a companion for me — one who shares my nature, with whom I might live in some sympathy. This you alone can do. I demand it as a right you cannot refuse.

panels.visual_direction: Tight close-up square panel, inset at right of Panel 2. Crops to Victor's face from brow to jaw. His expression holds three emotions simultaneously — pity, revulsion, and dread — none winning, all legible. Skin drawn gaunt, shadows pooling in hollows beneath his eyes and along his jaw, suggesting long illness and longer guilt. His eyes are wide not with mere fright but with a man confronting the full moral weight of what he has made. A single dark lock of hair is blown across his forehead by the alpine wind. The background is pure dark abstraction — a Mignola void with faint crosshatch texture suggesting cold. A sickly yellow-green watercolor tint washes his complexion, as though the creation has marked the creator in return. His lips are pressed shut. He has not yet spoken.
panels.narration: He was my making. Every grief in those eyes — mine.

panels.visual_direction: Wide horizontal panel, nearly half a page in height, bleeding to both edges. The Creature has shifted — no longer supplicating but standing fully upright, one arm raised not to strike but in a gesture of prophetic condemnation pointing outward into the waste. Victor is visible in the left quarter of the panel, smaller, slightly recoiled, his coat whipping violently in the wind. The glacier stretches vast between them, but now its Doré-precise crevasses read as open mouths, the ice ridges as teeth. The sky has darkened to near-black at the top of the frame; the last cold light catches only the Creature's upraised forearm and the terror in Victor's eyes. Heavy diagonal hatching across the glacier surface creates visual tension that pulls the eye from Victor to the Creature and back in an endless loop. A subtle Expressionist tilt to the horizon — perhaps four degrees — destabilizes the composition, making the ground itself feel unreliable. The Creature's shadow falls across the ice in an impossible, elongated shape that reaches toward Victor.
dialogue: THE CREATURE: I am what misery made me. Shunned by all mankind — even by you, who made me. Why should I pity your kind more than your kind has ever pitied me?

panels.visual_direction: Near-square close-up panel — the most emotionally concentrated image in the scene. The Creature's enormous hand fills most of the frame, extended palm-upward in desperate appeal rather than threat. Rendered with clinical anatomical precision in the Doré tradition: visible tendons raised beneath yellow, taut skin; bones massive beneath the surface; a faint line of dark stitching along the wrist where flesh once met flesh. The gesture itself is heartbreaking — open, vulnerable, asking. In the upper-left corner, slightly soft-focus and rendered in finer ink lines, Victor's smaller hand hangs at his side, not reaching back. The contrast between the two hands — one enormous and yearning, one human and withheld — is the moral center of the scene. A watercolor bleed of pale amber warms the Creature's palm: the only warmth in the entire sequence.
dialogue: THE CREATURE: I ask only for one like myself. One who will not turn away.

panels.visual_direction: Vertical panel mirroring Panel 2 in proportions but opposite in emotional register. Victor stands alone in the left half of the frame, three-quarter rear view, facing slightly away from the reader — his shoulders bent, his whole body expressing total, exhausted capitulation. His face is turned just enough that one eye is visible in profile, cast downward toward the ice. The Creature looms in the right half of the frame, not touching, watching — his posture now stilled, his expression unreadable, waiting. The glacier behind them has receded into near-abstraction: dark, impressionistic strokes of ink and grey watercolor wash, only a few precise Doré-style ice ridges remaining in the far distance to anchor the world. There is no visible light source; the panel is lit by implication alone, all heavy shadow and cold. The composition is deliberately unresolved — nothing is finished, everything has been agreed, and it is a horror. A thin hairline crack in the ice runs between the two figures, bisecting the ground on which they stand.
dialogue: VICTOR: ...I will do it.
panels.narration: And so I bound myself. Not with chains — with a word, spoken into the cold.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page one: Panel 1 is a wide establishing shot spanning the full page width (top tier). Panels 2 and 3 share the middle tier as equal halves. Panel 4 is a narrow, violent horizontal slash across the bottom — almost a wound across the page. Page two: Panel 5 is a tall, narrow vertical panel on the left (the window, the Creature's face). Panel 6 is a large, near-full-page panel on the right — the confrontation of gazes. The gutters between panels should be thick and black, like ink bleeding into the page, emphasizing claustrophobia and doom. No panel borders on Panel 6 — the image bleeds to the page edge, as if the Creature's grief cannot be contained.

panels.visual_direction: Wide establishing shot. A stone-walled workshop on a remote island — low vaulted ceiling, a single arched window rattling with storm. Rain streaks the glass in diagonal lines. Candlelight is the only warmth, pooling in amber circles that barely hold back the dark. Center-frame: Victor hunches over a long worktable, his back slightly to us, shoulders curved inward like a man bracing for a blow. On the table, barely visible but unmistakable in silhouette — a half-assembled female form, draped in shadow. Surgical instruments catch candlelight. The composition should feel like a Doré engraving of Dante's descent: ordered, architectural, but radiating dread. The storm outside presses at every edge of the frame. Victor's silhouette is gaunt, almost skeletal.
panels.narration: The Orkney Islands. Midnight. He was almost finished.

panels.visual_direction: Tight close-up on Victor's face — three-quarter angle, lit from below by candle. His eyes are wide and glassy, pupils dilated. Sweat glistens on his brow. His expression is the precise moment when certainty collapses into horror — not yet action, but the thought arriving like a wound. His jaw is set but trembling. Crosshatched shadows carve deep hollows under his cheekbones and eyes. He looks like a man seeing, for the first time, exactly what he has become. His gaze is directed downward — toward the body on the table — but his focus seems inward, somewhere far worse.
panels.narration: What was he making? Not a companion. A dynasty of devils.

panels.visual_direction: Close on Victor's hands, hovering over the female form — trembling, fingers splayed, neither touching nor retreating. The female body is shown abstractly: curves of pale material, a suggestion of assembled limbs, one slack hand with fingers not yet fully formed. Victor's hands are surgeon's hands gone wrong — capable, shaking, complicit. The candle beside them gutters in an unseen draft. The shadow of his hands falls across the body like a cage. Ink-heavy chiaroscuro: the body is half-light, half-dark, unfinished in every sense. A watercolor wash of sickly yellow bleeds across the form.
panels.narration: His promise. Her existence. The children they would make. He saw them all at once — and felt his mind crack.

panels.visual_direction: A full-width, low-height violent action panel — almost a horizontal slash across the bottom of the page. The visual is pure kinetic chaos: Victor mid-destruction, arms sweeping, instruments flying, the female form being torn apart in savage jagged motion. Use heavy diagonal ink lines and expressionist distortion — his face is a mask of revulsion and madness, mouth open in a soundless cry. The candlelight swings wildly, throwing lurching shadows. Objects are mid-air: a glass jar shattering, a surgical tool spinning, a piece of the unfinished body flung into darkness. The panel border itself seems to fracture at the edges, as if the violence is breaking the page. No clean lines — everything is slashes and smears.
dialogue: With a sensation of madness — I tore it apart.

panels.visual_direction: Tall, narrow vertical panel. The arched window from outside — we are now in the dark, in the storm, looking in. Rain obscures the glass in streaking diagonals. Pressed against the pane: the Creature's face. Enormous, filling the frame. His pale yellow eyes wide with anguish — he has seen everything. His breath fogs the glass. His massive hands press flat against the stone on either side of the window. In the background through the glass, barely visible: the wreckage of the worktable, the scattered remains. His expression is not rage yet — it is grief in its purest, most devastating form. The moment before fury. Mignola-style: face mostly shadow, the eyes carrying all the light.
panels.narration: He had been watching. He had seen everything.
sound_effects: HRAAAAAAH (a sound beginning, not yet fully formed)

panels.visual_direction: The largest panel — bleeds to all edges, no border. Split composition: on the left, the Creature outside the window, face now twisted from grief into terrible rage, mouth open in a howl, eyes burning like coals in deep shadow. On the right, Victor inside — frozen at the wreckage of the worktable, staring back through the glass. Their eyes meet across the pane, across the storm. The glass between them is the thinnest possible barrier — and both know it means nothing. Victor's face: white, hollow, already knowing what he has done. The Creature's mouth is open, and from it — rendered not as a sound effect but as caption text styled like a whisper — comes the promise. The composition is a mirror of two ruined men, the glass their last shared boundary. Everything is dark watercolor and heavy ink, but the Creature's eyes glow with an eerie amber that echoes the candle — as if he has taken Victor's light into himself and made it something terrible.
dialogue: You dare destroy my hopes?
It is well. I go. But remember — I shall be with you on your wedding night.
panels.narration: The words were barely sound. They were a sentence. Passed. Final.

panel_scripts.scene_title: The Destruction of the Best Hope
panel_scripts.layout_notes: This scene demands a two-page spread with six panels of deliberately escalating weight. Page one (panels 1–3): a triptych of dread building to the doorway reveal. Panel 1 is a wide horizontal establishing shot across the top third of the page — cinematic and cold. Panels 2 and 3 sit beneath it, equal width, intimate and oppressive. Page two (panels 4–6): Panel 4 is a full-width BLEED panel — the most important image in the scene — Elizabeth on the bed, the moonlight, the terrible stillness. It should occupy the top half of page two entirely. Panel 5 is a narrow vertical panel on the lower left: the Creature at the window. Panel 6, lower right, is a tight square: Victor's face alone. These final three panels must feel like the three notes of a death knell. Heavy black gutters throughout. No white space — this page should feel airless, suffocating.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE HORIZONTAL ESTABLISHING SHOT. The exterior of a Swiss lakeside inn at deep night — stone walls, peaked gables, a single upper window blazing with warm candlelight against a vast, cold, moonlit sky. The lake beyond is a sheet of hammered pewter. Storm clouds mass at the horizon, lit from beneath by distant lightning. The building is dwarfed by the landscape — the sublime pressing in from all sides. Victor's silhouette is barely visible through the lit window, pacing. The inn looks like a Gothic stage set: beautiful, isolated, doomed. Art style: Doré-esque engraving precision — every slate tile and ripple on the lake cross-hatched, the sky scraped with fine parallel lines. The candlelit window is the only warm tone on the page; everything else is blue-black ink and cold silver wash.
panels.narration: We had taken rooms at a small inn on the lake's edge. The night was still. I believed myself the guardian of all I loved.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT — interior corridor, low angle. Victor moves through a narrow stone hallway, a pistol held low at his side, a single candle in his other hand. His face is taut with vigilance, eyes cutting to every shadow. He is formally dressed — it is his wedding night — but his cravat is already loosened, his coat rumpled. The candlelight throws his shadow enormous and jagged against the wall behind him. Doors line the corridor; one at the far end stands slightly ajar. The perspective is slightly tilted — a diagonal lean in the architecture, expressionist, unsteady. Art style: Mignola-esque — massive blacks swallow the ceiling and floor; Victor exists in a narrow tunnel of sickly yellow candlelight. His elongated shadow is almost monstrous. The pistol catches a cold highlight.
panels.narration: I searched every passage. Every room. Told myself: he is here, he is near — and I would be ready.

panels.visual_direction: CLOSE-UP — Victor's hand on a door handle, pressing it open. The crack of the door admits a wedge of silver-blue moonlight that falls across Victor's face and chest. His expression shifts here: the vigilant tension drops away, replaced by something that has not yet become horror — a fraction of a second before understanding arrives. His eyes are wide, locked on something inside the room we cannot yet see. The candlelight in his other hand gutters violently — a window in the room beyond must be open. The candle flame bends toward him, as if recoiling. Art style: extreme chiaroscuro — the moonlight wedge is a hard geometric intrusion, almost surgical. Victor's face is half-lit, half-consumed by shadow, expressionistically distorted as if the architecture itself is reacting to what lies within.

FULL-WIDTH BLEED PANEL — the bridal chamber. This is the scene's heart and must be given maximum space. The room is flooded with cold moonlight from a wide-open window, curtains billowing inward like a shroud. The bed dominates the center of the composition: Elizabeth lies across it, her white wedding gown spread around her, golden hair fanned across the white bedclothes in terrible, almost painterly beauty. Her neck bears the dark marks of strangulation; her head falls at an unnatural angle, half-covered by her own hair. One arm trails to the floor. Her eyes are closed. She looks asleep — almost peaceful — which makes it worse. Victor stands in the doorway at the left edge of the panel, hand still on the door frame. The pistol has slipped from his grip; we see it mid-fall beside his foot, a blur of motion in a perfectly still image. His body is rigid, his mouth slightly open — he cannot scream, cannot move, cannot breathe. The room is immaculate except for one overturned vase of white flowers, water spreading across the stone floor. Art style: this panel should evoke a 19th-century academic oil painting in ink and watercolor — the composition deliberately mirrors Romantic deathbed iconography (Henry Wallis, John Millais). The moonlight is a watercolor bleed of cold blue-silver across white. Elizabeth's figure is rendered with exquisite anatomical care and terrible stillness. Victor is the only element of psychological distortion — his figure slightly elongated, his shadow reaching back out into the corridor as if trying to flee without him.
panels.narration: She was there. Lifeless. Thrown across the bed — her pale features half-covered by her hair.
sound_effects: CLATTER — the pistol strikes the floor

panels.visual_direction: NARROW VERTICAL PANEL — the open window, low angle looking up. The Creature fills the window frame from outside, enormous against the moonlit sky, gripping the stone sill with both massive hands. He is backlit — a silhouette of terrible size, every jagged, outsized proportion clear: the too-long arms, the broad shoulders, the towering height. His face catches a slant of moonlight: the watery pale eyes, the straight black lips drawn back in a grin that is not joy — it is a grimace of completion, of terrible grief weaponized into vengeance. He is pointing — one long finger aimed directly at Victor, directly at us. His yellow skin is taut across the bones of his face. Behind him: the open lake, moonlight on black water, the infinite indifferent dark. Art style: full Mignola silhouette — the Creature is 80% black ink, his form a void cut from the moonlit sky. Only the face catches light, rendered in precise, hideous detail: the engraving lines deep and deliberate, the eyes two pale watercolor washes of sickly yellow-white. The pointing finger is the compositional arrow that drives the reader's eye from this panel back to Panel 4.
panels.narration: At the open window — a figure. Vast. Grinning. He pointed, as if to name what he had done.

panels.visual_direction: TIGHT CLOSE-UP — Victor's face only, from just below the eyes to the chin. His eyes lock on the Creature. This is not rage. It is not grief, not yet. It is the moment before the mind accepts what the eyes have given it — total, white, annihilating devastation. One tear tracks down his left cheek, catching the moonlight. His jaw is set but trembling. His eyes are dry except for that one tear — wide, dark, the pupils blown fully open. The skin beneath them is hollow, shadowed. This face is the face of a man watching his soul leave his body. Art style: maximum expressionist distortion — the face fills the panel entirely, no background, the ink lines around the eyes drawn with the same crosshatch density as a Doré crowd scene, every line of grief carved in. The single tear is a clean watercolor wash, the only soft mark on an otherwise brutally hard-inked face. No speech bubble. No caption. The face says everything.
panels.narration: Why did I not die then? Why am I left — to carry this?

panel_scripts.scene_title: Victor's Death and the Creature's Farewell
panel_scripts.layout_notes: Six panels across two pages. Page 1: Panel 1 is a wide establishing shot spanning the full page width (top tier). Below it, Panels 2 and 3 share equal space in a two-column grid. Page 2: Panel 4 is a tall, narrow vertical panel on the left — almost a column — forcing the eye downward. Panel 5 is a mid-width close-up beside it. Panel 6 is a full-width bleed panel at the bottom of the page — the ice plain — borderless, fading into white at the edges. Heavy blacks dominate throughout; the oil lamp is the only warm color in the entire spread. All borders should feel like steel engravings — precise, inked rules — except the final panel, which has no border at all.

panels.visual_direction: WIDE ESTABLISHING SHOT — full page width, low ceiling. Victor's cramped ship cabin rendered with Doré-level architectural precision: exposed timber ribs, a frosted porthole glazed with ice crystals, a guttering oil lamp casting a small ellipse of amber light in an ocean of shadow. On the narrow bunk, Victor lies still — face upturned, eyes closed, the terrible anguish finally erased, almost beautiful in death. His hands are folded at his chest, skeletal fingers interlaced. Dominating the left side of the frame, the Creature kneels beside the bunk — enormous, his head nearly touching the low ceiling, his massive frame grotesquely mismatched with the tiny cabin. Both hands cover his face. His shoulders are heaving. The crosshatching on the Creature's coat is dense and ravaged — every stitch a scar. Walton is a small, rigid silhouette in the open doorway at the far right — the corridor behind him a rectangle of cold blue-white light. He does not move. Caption box in upper-left corner.
panels.narration: He was already there.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM CLOSE-UP — Walton's face in the doorway, half-lit by the corridor light behind him, half-consumed by the cabin's shadow. His expression is not horror exactly — it is the face of a man whose world has just been restructured. Eyes wide, jaw slightly parted, one hand still gripping the door frame. The German Expressionist angle tilts slightly, the door frame diagonal, the corridor behind him receding at a vertiginous slant. He is the reader's surrogate: we see what he sees, we feel what he cannot yet name.
panels.narration: I had braced myself for death. I had not braced myself for this.

panels.visual_direction: MEDIUM SHOT — The Creature looks up. This is the emotional fulcrum of the scene and must be rendered with absolute precision. His face is not the monstrous mask of nightmare — it is ravaged, open, stripped. Watery pale-yellow eyes rimmed red with grief, the dun-white skin pulled taut with anguish, the straight black lips parted. His enormous hands have fallen from his face and rest on the edge of Victor's bunk — the dead man's skeletal hand inches from the Creature's. They do not quite touch. The oil lamp is positioned behind the Creature's shoulder, giving him an involuntary halo — ironic, devastating. He speaks. The speech bubble is ragged at the edges, as if torn from the air.
dialogue: That is also my victim. In his murder... my crimes are consummated.

panels.visual_direction: TALL VERTICAL PANEL — the Creature standing now, filling the full height of the panel, his head bent to avoid the ceiling. He faces Walton, who is still frozen in the doorway below-frame. This is a Mignola-esque composition: the Creature rendered as pure mass and silhouette except for the face — which the lamp catches in terrible detail. He gestures with one open hand toward Victor's body (just visible at the panel's lower edge). The cabin walls press in on both sides, the wood grain crosshatched into suffocation. The speech bubbles stack vertically, one below the other, descending like falling stones.
dialogue: I, the abandoned — I am an abortion, to be spurned and trampled on.
He suffered not in the dying. Not the ten-thousandth part of what I suffered in the living.

panels.visual_direction: CLOSE-UP — The Creature at the porthole. He has turned from Walton. One enormous hand grips the porthole frame; the other rests flat against the frozen glass, fingers spread. Through the porthole: pure white void — the Arctic, featureless and absolute. His profile is in sharp silhouette against that whiteness — the irregular contours of his assembled face, the heavy brow, the black lips. His eye, just visible, catches the white light. He is already leaving. The speech bubble curves gently, as though exhaled rather than spoken.
dialogue: Soon these burning miseries will be extinct. I shall ascend my funeral pile... and exult in the agony of the flames.
panels.narration: He did not look at me again. He looked only at the ice.

panels.visual_direction: FULL-WIDTH BORDERLESS BLEED PANEL — the final image. The Arctic ice plain stretches to every edge of the page, rendered in Doré's engraving style: an infinite field of fractured white, receding in careful perspective lines toward a horizon that bleeds into unprinted paper. At the center-left of the frame — already small, already receding — the Creature's dark figure moves away from us. His shape is unmistakable: that enormous silhouette, those unnatural proportions. But he is small now. A black mark on white silence. Around him at the margins, the blizzard begins — loose expressionist watercolor washes in pale grey and ice-blue creeping inward from the edges, blurring the ice plain, softening the horizon. He is already being erased. There is no speech bubble. There is no caption. There is only the figure, the ice, and the dark that is coming.
